desc:
A workshop has two machines, A and B. Every job jobs[i] = [a, b] must first be processed on machine A for a time units and, once that is finished, on machine B for b time units. Each machine handles one job at a time without interruption. Machine B can start a job only after A has completely finished it, and it may sit idle while waiting. Both machines process the jobs in the same order, which you choose (for two machines this is without loss of optimality). Everything starts at time 0.

Return the minimum possible time at which the last job leaves machine B.

jobs = [[3, 2], [1, 4]]  ->  7

Order [1,4] then [3,2]: A finishes them at 1 and 4; B runs the first during 1..5 and the second during 5..7. The other order gives 9.
hints: With a fixed order the finish times are easy to simulate: tA += a; tB = max(tB, tA) + b. The whole difficulty is choosing the order.
You want machine B to start working as early as possible and never starve. Which jobs should go first: those that are quick on A, or those that are slow on A?
Johnson's rule. Jobs with a < b go first, sorted by a ascending; the remaining jobs (a ≥ b) go afterwards, sorted by b descending.
editorial: This is the classic two-machine flow shop, solved by Johnson's rule. Split the jobs into group 1 (a < b) and group 2 (a ≥ b). Run group 1 first in increasing order of a, so machine B gets fed as early as possible, then group 2 in decreasing order of b, so the jobs that are short on B and cannot keep it busy are placed last, when machine A is already finished and only B's tail remains.

To get the answer, simulate the chosen order: tA += a; tB = max(tB, tA) + b for each job, and return tB. The correctness proof is an exchange argument on neighbouring jobs: job i should precede job j whenever min(ai, bj) ≤ min(aj, bi), and Johnson's order realises exactly that. Sorting dominates: O(n log n).
solution:
def minMakespan(jobs):
    first = sorted((j for j in jobs if j[0] < j[1]), key=lambda j: j[0])
    second = sorted((j for j in jobs if j[0] >= j[1]), key=lambda j: -j[1])
    ta = tb = 0
    for a, b in first + second:
        ta += a
        tb = max(tb, ta) + b
    return tb
